title: Strings in a jazz context
summary: Strings speak late and fit poorly with a rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: It all depends what the engineer does. I latched onto that doing Broadway shows, because they never have enough strings. The trick is to always have them play under, never to play over but then when the engineer comes on, he puts them right up even, and the guys don't always watch it either, because they can't hear; they're always put in a place where they can't hear.
How do you feel about using strings in a jazz context? That's been a real problem for a lot of people.

I think jazz--the reason for that is that they speak later. Strings always speak late and you put that with a rhythm section which speaks immediately and it doesn't work; there's not a connective tissue there. The only thing they can do is play whole notes--
The only other way to do it is to take out the rhythm section (inaudible).
There was a rhythm section in Focus?
He was a soloist in one number.
That was the bone to the commercialism, why they put it in the album. He played solo.
Yes, considering the character of the other things you wrote for the record, drums would have been just so much surface noise, there is nothing for them to do.
No; or get in the way, even worse.
You notice the time flies all around? But that doesn't bother Stan.
It's almost like a rubato, or semi rubato sort of flavor to it.
That's the other thing, strings sound better if you allow them to do that, and it sounds very wooden if you don't. They don't fit well into that regimented thing.
